meta.description: The tools, skills and memory I use to run AI coding agents across 40+ repositories: ai-usagebar, ghpending, tclock, my-skills and ai-memory, plus my LLM benchmark.

hero.title: Akita's AI Toolkit
hero.lede: I maintain more than 40 open source repositories with AI agents doing most of the typing. These are the tools I built to keep that manageable, the workflow that ties them together, and the writing where I document what I learn.
hero.shotAlt: My second monitor: tclock showing 16:10:22 in large red digits, a GitHub pending widget listing open pull requests and issues for ai-memory and ai-usagebar, a Google Calendar widget and a system health strip.
hero.shotCaption: My second monitor on a normal Thursday. 43 repositories checked, 6 with something waiting.
hero.portraitAlt: Illustrated portrait of Fabio Akita: grey hair, round glasses, white shirt and a dark tie, looking up with a confident half smile.
hero.intro: I am Fabio Akita: a programmer for more than 30 years, entrepreneur, speaker, writer and former YouTuber. My LinkedIn has the long version.

desk.title: One desk, two monitors, many agents
desk.lede: The second monitor tells me what needs attention. The first one runs one agent per project. A shared memory sits under all of them, and a gauge in the top bar tells me when to change providers.
desk.alt: Two monitors on a desk. Monitor 2 shows a red pixel clock and a ghpending list. Monitor 1 shows tmux split into four agent panes, with ai-usagebar in the top bar. A teal slab labelled ai-memory under the desk feeds all four panes.

steps.title: Monitor 2: the queue
steps.text: tclock shows the time, my calendar, system health, and a ghpending widget with every open pull request and issue across the repositories I track.

steps.title: Monitor 1: tmux, one agent per project
steps.text: Each tmux window is a project. I start the agent with ai-memory run and give it one line: run pr-audit and iss-audit, then run github-resolution. The skills do the rest.

steps.title: Under everything: ai-memory
steps.text: Every project keeps its own memory of decisions and traps. A new session starts where the last one stopped, whichever agent runs it.

steps.title: In the top bar: ai-usagebar
steps.text: ai-usagebar shows how much of each plan's 5-hour and weekly quota I have used, and when it resets. When one runs dry, I move the work to another agent.

loop.title: The daily loop
loop.lede: The skills do the heavy lifting. I read their reports and make the calls.
loop.alt: A clockwise loop of five stations: See what is pending, Audit, Resolve, Release and Kaizen, around a central ai-memory wiki connected to every step.
loop.caption: ghpending shows the queue, the audit skills check every pull request and issue, github-resolution turns the approved ones into merged code, and the release skill cuts a version when I ask for one. Kaizen closes the circle: whatever went wrong becomes a fix to the process itself.

quote.text: Ship first, fix later. AI made fixing faster and cheaper.

switch.title: Out of quota? Change agents, keep the context
switch.lede: The memory lives outside the agent, so moving a task from Claude Code to Codex or OpenCode costs one command. The new agent reads the same wiki the previous one wrote.
switch.alt: Three terminals: Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode. Claude Code's quota gauge is full and red. A green arrow labelled Switch moves the work to Codex. All three sit on one slab labelled Same memory.
switch.post: The blog post on switching agents

tools.title: Three small tools I use every day
tools.lede: In order of how much I depend on them. All three are written in Rust, MIT licensed, and install with one command.

items.tagline: Know how much AI you have left
items.text: A top-bar widget, a terminal UI and native tray apps that show quota, balance and reset time for Claude, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Z.AI, OpenRouter and 19 more providers.
points: Omarchy Quattro, Waybar, GNOME, KDE Plasma 6, macOS and Windows
A desktop alert when a quota window crosses 97%
One bar item can cycle through every provider you pay for
items.shotAlt: The ai-usagebar panel open in the Omarchy top bar, showing Z.AI GLM Coding Pro usage: session, weekly and monthly MCP tools, each with its reset time, and tabs for Claude, Codex, Z.AI, OpenRouter and Kimi.

items.tagline: Every open PR and issue, in one list
items.text: A Rust CLI that fetches every repository you track at once and prints what is waiting. Your own items drop to the bottom, since they wait on other people. Forks show your pull requests on the upstream project instead.
points: Dependabot, secret scanning and code scanning alerts for repos you own
Sort by activity, name, count or the most neglected
Doubles as a tclock widget, with matching themes
items.shotAlt: ghpending output in a terminal: repositories FrankClaw, FrankMD, FrankMega and FrankSherlock, each with its open pull requests and issues, number, title, age and author.

items.tagline: A clock for the second monitor
items.text: My maintained fork of clock-tui: a terminal clock, timer, stopwatch and countdown. Widgets run any command and show its output under the clock, so the clock becomes a dashboard.
points: Evangelion and NERV themes, cycled with Shift+T
Widgets refresh on their own schedule and can open detail popups
Prebuilt binaries for x86_64 and aarch64
items.shotAlt: tclock with the NERV theme: 17:34:24 in large red pixel digits over a dark sky, a GitHub pending widget, a Google Calendar widget and a system health strip.

sisters.title: The bigger pieces
sisters.lede: Two of my tools grew large enough for their own sites. The third is the set of prompts that drives the whole pipeline.

items.title: ai-memory
items.text: Long-term memory for coding agents: a git-backed wiki of plain Markdown that captures sessions, consolidates decisions and hands work from one agent to another.

items.title: ai-jail
items.text: An OS sandbox for AI coding agents on Linux and macOS. The project stays writable. Your keys, tokens and home directory stay out of reach.

items.title: my-skills
items.text: About two dozen agent skills, from pr-audit to release. Published so you can read the reasoning and write your own.

writing.title: Learning in the open
writing.lede: Everything I try with AI ends up on my blog, with the numbers, the bills and the failures. That is also how I decide which model to use for what.
writing.postsTitle: A few posts that show how I work

quote.text: Your excitement about AI is inversely proportional to your knowledge of AI.
quote.original: Sua empolgação com IA é inversamente proporcional ao seu conhecimento sobre IA.

newsletter.title: And every Monday, a newsletter
newsletter.text: The M.Akita Chronicles is a weekly tech newsletter and podcast in Portuguese, curated by me and commented on by M.Arvin, a very depressed robot. The podcast now also has some of my favorite blog posts as full episodes.

independence.title: Nobody pays me to say any of this
independence.text: I am not a paid content creator. I take no sponsorships, have no Patreon and no paid subscriptions, and I do not make money from views. I am self-sustained, and I do all of this for my own pleasure. When I recommend a tool or a model, it is because I use it.

quote.text: I only believe in voluntary trade for mutual benefit.

podcasts.title: Five long conversations, on video
podcasts.text: Flow, Inteligência Ltda, Fernando Ulrich and a Tropical on Rails talk: hours about AI, programming jobs and the hype, plus the short cuts if you are in a hurry.

contact.title: How to contact me
contact.warning: Do not try to sell me anything, and do not offer sponsorships: I will not answer those. There is no automatic "received" reply. If I do not answer, I was not interested.
